title: Boeing Knew What the 737 Max Could Do at Low Speed. The Pilots Were Never Told the System Existed.
title_candidates: Boeing Knew What the 737 Max Could Do at Low Speed. The Pilots Were Never Told the System Existed.
Boeing Knew the 737 Max Could Push Its Own Nose Down. The Pilots Were Never Told the System Existed.
The Federal Aviation Administration Ran the Numbers on the 737 Max. It Let the Fleet Keep Flying for Five Months.
description:
Over the Java Sea, a wheel beside the captain's knee turns by itself. He was never told it could. Who decided he did not need to know?

On the evening of the twenty-eighth of October, 2018, a Boeing 737 MAX left Denpasar for Jakarta. One sensor on the outside of the fuselage was reporting the wrong angle, wrong by about twenty-one degrees, and it stayed wrong. The stick shaker ran for the whole flight. Ninety-six minutes.

Then the nose went down on its own. The captain decided this was a runaway stabiliser, and cut the electricity to the trim. They landed. Everybody walked off. That crew was able to land the aeroplane while experiencing the same conditions as the flight that crashed.

Because the next morning, the same aeroplane took off again. More than twenty times, that wheel turned itself down, and two men turned it back up, and neither of them knew what they were fighting. Eleven minutes, from the runway to the sea.

Airlines do not really buy aeroplanes. They buy fleets, and a fleet is only cheap if every pilot can fly every aircraft in it. Level B training is a course a pilot can do on a laptop. Level D generally means the simulator. The 737 MAX was designed to land on Level B.

In December of 2011, Boeing signed a contract with Southwest Airlines that obliged Boeing to discount every MAX it delivered by at least one million dollars if the FAA required simulator training.

Boeing wrote a piece of software to push the nose back down and make the aeroplane feel like the old one. Its name was the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System. MCAS.

The 737 has two angle-of-attack vanes. MCAS listened to one. In March of 2016 Boeing redesigned MCAS to work at lower speeds too. As originally designed, it could move the horizontal stabiliser a maximum of zero point six degrees. The redesigned version could move it two point five. Boeing then asked the FAA to remove the references to MCAS from the manual in the cockpit. The FAA approved it. The pilots were never told the system existed.

On the fifteenth of November, 2016, one of Boeing's two 737 MAX technical pilots was flying the simulator and felt MCAS operate at low speed. That same day he messaged a colleague. Oh shocker alert. MCAS is now active down to point two. It's running rampant in the sim on me.

Boeing's own agreement, signed in a federal court, says the two men deceived the Aircraft Evaluation Group about the basis on which it had agreed to remove MCAS from the report. By the end of 2016, Boeing knew what the 737 MAX could do at low speed, and the Aircraft Evaluation Group did not.

One man was later tried, and a federal jury acquitted him on all four counts in less than two hours. He is not named here, and nothing in this film says he lied.

On the third of December, 2018, with an emergency airworthiness directive already in place but no fix to MCAS, the FAA finished a risk analysis on its own aeroplane. It indicated there could be more than fifteen fatal 737 MAX crashes over the estimated thirty-year lifetime of the fleet.

The Inspector General's office recorded that the calculated individual risk, two point six eight fatalities per million flight hours, remained below the guideline the method itself uses, and that these figures should not be viewed as predictive values. So the fleet kept flying, for five months.

On the tenth of March, 2019, Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 lifted off from Addis Ababa. This crew had the bulletin and the directive, and they did the procedure. They cut the power, and then they could not move the wheel by hand at all.

Three days later the 737 MAX was grounded in the United States. Ethiopia's investigators concluded that the repetitive, uncommanded nose-down inputs from MCAS were the most probable cause. The American investigators disagreed in writing, and said appropriate crew management of the event, using the procedures that existed at the time, would have allowed the crew to recover.

On the seventh of January, 2021, Boeing signed an agreement with the United States Department of Justice and agreed to pay two billion five hundred and thirteen million six hundred thousand dollars, in three parts. The agreement states what the criminal penalty represents: Boeing's own assessment of the cost of implementing full-flight simulator training for the 737 MAX.

On the sixth of November, 2025, the court granted the motion. The case was dismissed. Nobody was convicted of anything.

—

Prime Documentary makes long-form documentaries about ordinary people and the systems that fail around them. This episode is built from Boeing's 2021 agreement with the Department of Justice and its statement of facts, the Indonesian and Ethiopian accident reports, the House Committee's report and the Inspector General's review.

This film contains AI-assisted visualization: symbolic reconstruction, no real likenesses. Generated imagery is not evidence and is not presented as an authentic record.
